title: Stable risk adjustment identifies the direction and sharp size bounds of credibility revisions
scope: Two-announcement extension of the source's binary sovereign-pricing benchmark with a common relative state pricing kernel.
significance: Derives the exact common-kernel revision curve, identifies the sign despite unidentified credibility levels, and computes the sharp maximum probability change and bounded-kernel extrema.
body:
# Credibility revisions under stable risk adjustment

The source proves that a single bond price does not identify the physical implementation probability without risk-kernel restrictions. Two prices can nevertheless identify the direction of a credibility revision if the relative state pricing kernel is stable. Their exact joint restriction also bounds how large that revision can be.

For two communication regimes \(j=0,1\), recover risk-adjusted probabilities \(q_j\in(0,1)\) from the source's bond-pricing equation, using the corresponding known loss and risk-free rate. Suppose the positive conditional pricing-kernel ratio
\[
r=\frac{E[m_j\mid S=1]}{E[m_j\mid S=0]}
\]
is common across the two regimes. Its overall level may change consistently with each risk-free price. Define odds \(o_j=q_j/(1-q_j)>0\). The source's odds equation gives
\[
p_j(r)=\frac{o_j}{r+o_j}.
\tag{A}
\]
Thus the joint credibility set is this one-parameter curve. Independent choices from two marginal credibility intervals generally violate the common-\(r\) restriction.

Assume first \(q_1>q_0\), so \(o_1>o_0\). Their probability difference is
\[
\Delta p(r)=
\frac{r(o_1-o_0)}{(r+o_1)(r+o_0)}>0.
\tag{B}
\]
Hence a positive price-implied \(q\) revision identifies a positive physical credibility revision under stable relative risk adjustment, even when neither level is point identified.

Differentiation gives
\[
\Delta p'(r)=
\frac{(o_1-o_0)(o_0o_1-r^2)}
     {(r+o_1)^2(r+o_0)^2}.
\]
It increases up to \(r_*=\sqrt{o_0o_1}\) and decreases thereafter. Therefore, with no magnitude restriction beyond \(r>0\), the exact change set is
\[
\Delta p\in\left(
0,\frac{\sqrt{o_1}-\sqrt{o_0}}
        {\sqrt{o_1}+\sqrt{o_0}}
\right].
\tag{C}
\]
The maximum is attained at \(r_*\). The zero lower endpoint is approached as \(r\downarrow0\) or \(r\uparrow\infty\), but is not attained by a finite positive kernel ratio. Continuity on each side of the maximum proves that every intermediate value is attained.

If external information supplies \(r\in[\ell,u]\subset(0,\infty)\), both endpoints become attained. The minimum change is the smaller of \(\Delta p(\ell),\Delta p(u)\); the maximum is \(\Delta p\) at \(r_*\) clipped to that interval. Evaluating only adverse level endpoints would miss this interior maximum.

Sharpness follows by using the source's positive two-state pricing kernel separately in each regime:
\[
m_j(1)=q_j/(R_{f,j}p_j),\qquad
m_j(0)=(1-q_j)/(R_{f,j}(1-p_j)).
\]
Substitution of (A) gives state ratio exactly \(r\) in both regimes. These kernels reproduce both bond and risk-free prices, so the entire curve consists of admissible economies.

For \(q_0=1/5,q_1=4/5\), odds are \(1/4,4\), so \(r_*=1\) and the sharp maximum change is \(3/5\). The same price revision can correspond to an arbitrarily small positive physical revision if the unrestricted common ratio is extreme. If the two \(q\)'s coincide, the physical probabilities coincide; if their order reverses, interchange the regimes and negate the resulting interval.

Stable relative risk adjustment is a substantive exclusion: communication can itself alter state-contingent marginal valuations. Without it, the source's separate arbitrary-kernel constructions allow either sign. This result does not infer stability from randomized messages, identify actual implementation beliefs, or combine the pricing sector with the household saving model into a general equilibrium.

title: An exact joint durability polytope with a common bounded-outcome baseline
scope: Two active tutor-arm six-month mean effects under the source's common persistence parameter and bounded deviation restriction.
significance: Characterizes the sharp joint delayed-effect region, adding the essential common-baseline range restriction and proving constructive future-outcome realizability.
body:
# A joint durability polytope with one common baseline

The source correctly warns that a shared persistence parameter couples multiple tutor arms. Bounded outcomes impose an additional joint restriction: the two effects must use the same future comparator mean. Combining these restrictions gives an exact finite polytope for the mean-level durability class.

Let the identified early assistant-free effects be \(s_1,s_2\), and suppose the maintained bridge is
\[
\tau_j=\rho s_j+d_j,\qquad
\rho\in[\rho_L,\rho_U],\quad |d_j|\le\epsilon_j,\quad j=1,2.
\tag{A}
\]
The six-month outcomes \(Y(0),Y(1),Y(2)\) all lie in \([0,1]\). Assume no other temporal or outcome-level restrictions. In particular, (A) concerns effects, not a rank-preserving individual law linking early and future scores.

The exact joint set is the projection onto \((\tau_1,\tau_2)\) of
\[
\rho_L\le\rho\le\rho_U,\qquad
-\epsilon_j\le\tau_j-\rho s_j\le\epsilon_j,
\]
\[
-1\le\tau_j\le1,\qquad
|\tau_1-\tau_2|\le1.
\tag{B}
\]
It is a compact convex polytope when nonempty. If it is empty, the supplied bridge and bounded-score model are jointly rejected.

To prove the additional inequalities, write \(\mu_0=E Y(0)\), so the active means are \(\mu_0+\tau_1,\mu_0+\tau_2\). Three numbers in \([0,1]\) can differ by at most one. Thus each effect and their difference satisfy (B).

Conversely, given any effects obeying those range inequalities, a common baseline mean exists precisely when
\[
\max(0,-\tau_1,-\tau_2)
\le
\min(1,1-\tau_1,1-\tau_2).
\tag{C}
\]
The left side is the least baseline consistent with nonnegative arm means, and the right side is the greatest consistent with means at most one. Condition (C) is equivalent to
\[
\max(0,\tau_1,\tau_2)-\min(0,\tau_1,\tau_2)\le1,
\]
which in turn is exactly the three pairwise range restrictions in (B). Choose any such \(\mu_0\), and set future potential scores to the constants \(\mu_0,\mu_0+\tau_1,\mu_0+\tau_2\), respectively. They are bounded and realize the desired effects. Append these future outcomes to the complete observed early-data law without changing it. Since the only bridge is the mean condition (A), the chosen \(\rho,d_1,d_2\) make this a compatible continuation. This proves sharpness of the entire projected set.

A small example shows why coordinate intervals are insufficient even at a fixed persistence value. Let early effects be \(s_1=0.4,s_2=-0.4\), realized by early means \(0.5,0.9,0.1\). Set \(\rho=1\) and \(\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=0.6\). The separate delayed-effect intervals include \(\tau_1=0.8\) and \(\tau_2=-0.8\). Together those values are impossible: they require active means differing by \(1.6\). Inequality \(|\tau_1-\tau_2|\le1\) correctly removes that pair, even though both individual contrasts lie in \([-1,1]\).

Every linear joint question, such as the worst-case advantage of one tutor over another, is a linear program over (B). This preserves the common persistence and baseline rather than combining extrema from different continuations. Sampling uncertainty in the early effects requires retaining their simultaneous confidence set as well; the population polytope alone is not a confidence statement.

This result does not validate a six-month persistence bridge, estimate delayed learning, or remove classroom interference and attrition concerns. It supplies an exact realizability refinement inside the source's explicitly stated mean-level sensitivity model.

title: Fair weather-index insurance can overinsure adapted farmers
scope: Separate fixed weather-index contract extension of the source's CARA farmer model, with correct beliefs and fair premium independent of realized adaptation losses.
significance: Derives the exact adoption threshold, proves overinsurance can reverse monotone coverage welfare for adapters, and solves joint coverage/adaptation choice.
body:
# Weather-index insurance and overinsurance after adaptation

The manuscript proves monotone welfare gains from higher fair indemnity coverage, where payment and premium track the actual loss after adaptation. It explicitly notes that a fixed weather-index contract has a different incentive formula. That alternative can be solved exactly and shows why the monotonicity should not be transferred across contract types.

Keep true drought probability \(p\in(0,1)\), CARA parameter \(\rho>0\), loss \(L>0\), adaptation loss reduction \(d\in(0,L)\), and cost \(K>0\). Maintain correct beliefs and financial feasibility of both adoption choices. Replace the indemnity by a weather payment \(qLZ\), with actuarially fair premium \(qpL\), independent of whether the farmer adapts. Coverage satisfies \(q\in[0,1]\). Consumption becomes
\[
c(D,Z)=W-KD-qpL-\{L-dD-qL\}Z.
\tag{A}
\]
The source's \(W>K+L\) is sufficient to keep consumption positive throughout.

Extend its risk function to all real \(x\):
\[
\psi_p(x)=\rho^{-1}\log(1-p+pe^{\rho x}).
\]
The exponential moment is finite for every finite \(x\). The actual certainty equivalent is
\[
CE(D,q)=W-KD-qpL-\psi_p((1-q)L-dD).
\]
Thus adaptation is optimal, with the source's adoption-at-tie convention, exactly when
\[
K\le B_I(q):=
\psi_p((1-q)L)-\psi_p((1-q)L-d).
\tag{B}
\]
There is no premium-reduction term \(qpd\): the premium does not fall after adaptation.

Since \(\psi_p'\) is strictly increasing,
\[
B_I'(q)=-L\{\psi_p'((1-q)L)-\psi_p'((1-q)L-d)\}<0.
\]
At no insurance, this agrees with the source's uninsured threshold. At full index coverage,
\[
B_I(1)=-\psi_p(-d)<pd.
\tag{C}
\]
The strict inequality follows from strict Jensen convexity:
\(\psi_p(-d)>E[-dZ]=-pd\). Full index coverage therefore suppresses adaptation more strongly than full loss indemnity, whose threshold in the source is exactly \(pd\). For any \(K\) strictly between \(B_I(1)\) and \(pd\), full indemnity induces adoption while full index coverage does not.

The welfare difference is also exact. For a fixed decision \(D\),
\[
\partial_q CE(D,q)
=L\{\psi_p'(L-dD-qL)-p\}.
\tag{D}
\]
The derivative is positive when \(q<1-dD/L\), zero at equality, and negative above it, because \(\psi_p'(0)=p\). Without adaptation the optimum is full coverage. With adaptation the optimum is \(q_D=1-d/L<1\): higher coverage creates a net positive drought payoff and overinsures the reduced physical loss. Consequently further fair index coverage beyond that point lowers the adapted farmer's welfare. This is a contract-specific reversal of monotonicity, not an error in the source's indemnity theorem.

If coverage and adaptation can be chosen jointly, each decision uses
\[
q_D=(L-dD)/L.
\]
Residual drought risk then vanishes, and the optimized certainty equivalent is
\[
CE_D^*=W-KD-p(L-dD).
\]
The joint optimum adopts exactly when \(K\le pd\), with equal values at equality. Thus freely adjustable fair index coverage implements full hedging of the actual residual loss; forcing the same maximum coverage across farmers need not do so.

This extension assumes perfect alignment of the weather trigger with loss occurrence, known \(p\), no loading and adjustable coverage. Basis risk, liquidity constraints and insurer participation with hidden adaptation can alter the solution. It does not estimate an insurance effect or extrapolate a current trial to a new climate. It identifies a precise contract-design boundary already signaled by the manuscript.
